title: Turn the roadmap into a delivery plan
summary: A delivery plan shows how the first release will actually get built: the order of work, the milestones, who is needed and what could get in the way. It turns intentions into commitments the team believes in.

beginner: Start from the ordered backlog for the first release. Ask the team to size the epics roughly, for example small, medium or large.
Group the work into a few milestones, each one something you could demonstrate, such as 'a user can sign up' or 'payments work end to end'.
Check the team's real capacity: holidays, other commitments and support work. Plan for about 70 to 80 percent of their time, not 100.
List dependencies on other teams, suppliers and approvals, and agree dates with them.
Write down the top risks and what you will do if each one happens.
Share a simple plan with ranges, such as 'June to July', rather than single dates, and agree how often you will update it.
intermediate: Size epics with the team and group them into demonstrable milestones.
Plan against real capacity and agree cross-team dependencies.
Record risks with owners and mitigations.
Publish a plan with date ranges and a regular update rhythm.
experienced: Use past team throughput, not optimism, to forecast, and show confidence levels.
Sequence work to retire the biggest delivery risks first.
Agree explicit trade-off rules with stakeholders: which of scope, date and quality moves first.
Keep the plan live and re-forecast as soon as reality changes.

canDelegateTo.task: Build the plan, track capacity and manage dependencies
Size the epics and identify technical risks

toolExamples.jira: Use a timeline view to place epics against milestones and show dependencies between them.
toolExamples.azure-devops: Use delivery plans to see each team's work and dependencies on one timeline.
toolExamples.linear: Set project target dates and milestones, and link blocking issues across teams.
toolExamples.confluence: Keep a release planning page with the team, goals, non-goals, milestones and risks.

definitionOfDone: Milestones agreed and each one demonstrable
Plan based on real capacity, with dependencies agreed
Plan shared with date ranges and an update rhythm
pitfalls: Planning to 100 percent of the team's time
Finding out about a dependency when it blocks the team

leaderView.good: Delivery plans show the order of work, milestones, owners and risks, and are kept up to date.
ask: What's the next milestone, and how confident are we?
What's the biggest risk to the date?
signs: Plans are only revisited when a date slips.
Risks are known in the team but not shared upwards.
